sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
How fast can a transistor be? The standard figure of merit is the **unity-gain frequency** \(f_T\). Drive the gate with a small-signal current, hold the drain at a fixed DC voltage so it is an AC short, and compare the drain current with the gate current. At low frequency the ratio is enormous, because the gate draws almost nothing. As frequency rises, the gate current \(j\omega(C_{gs} + C_{gd})v_{gs}\) grows while the drain current \(g_mv_{gs}\) stays put. The ratio falls at 20 dB per decade and crosses 1 at \(f_T\).

Shorting the output is deliberate: it removes any load and any Miller multiplication. That makes \(f_T\) a property of the device and its bias, useful for comparing technologies. For a long-channel device the width and oxide cancel. What remains is \(\mu V_{ov}/L^2\), so short channels and larger overdrives are fast. Real amplifiers have source resistance and voltage gain, so their bandwidths sit well below \(f_T\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ \left|\frac{i_{out}}{i_{in}}\right| \approx \frac{g_m}{\omega(C_{gs} + C_{gd})} = \frac{f_T}f, \qquad f_T = \frac{g_m}{2\pi(C_{gs} + C_{gd})} \]
\[ \omega_T \approx \frac{g_m}{C_{gs}} = \frac32\frac{\mu_nV_{ov}}{L^2} \quad (\text{long channel}, C_{gd} \ll C_{gs}) \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A device with \(g_m = 3\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(C_{gs} = 36\ \mathrm{fF}\) and \(C_{gd} = 9\ \mathrm{fF}\) has \(f_T = 3\ \mathrm{mS}/(2\pi\cdot45\ \mathrm{fF}) \approx 10.6\ \mathrm{GHz}\). At 1 GHz its current gain is still about 10.6. A version with half the channel length at the same overdrive would, by long-channel scaling, reach roughly four times that \(f_T\).

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Measuring with the drain loaded or open; \(f_T\) is defined with the output shorted.
- Dropping the \(2\pi\) when converting \(g_m/C\) to hertz.
- Expecting \(f_T\) to rise with width; \(g_m\) and \(C_{gs}\) both scale with \(W\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: \(f_T\) is the yardstick for every frequency-response result that follows: Miller-limited CS stages, nearly-\(f_T\) followers, and cascades that split gain to recover bandwidth.
